title: Five Ways to Turn a Stimulus into a Current

scenes.visual: Title card: Five Ways to Turn a Stimulus into a Current. Show stimulus → channel current → electrical signal.

scenes.tts: Every sensory cell turns a stimulus into a change in ion channel current. That is how force, chemicals or heat become an electrical signal. But the machinery between stimulus and current differs. Some routes couple the stimulus directly to a pore. Others insert enzymes, or add an output channel. Comparing those routes explains how a cell detects a stimulus and passes the message on.

Comparing those routes explains how a cell detects a stimulus and passes the message on.

scenes.visual: Build the stimulus → channel current → electrical signal map. Branch it into direct gating, an enzyme cascade and a receptor cell with a separate output channel. Keep detection and output as successive stages where appropriate.

scenes.tts: In a hair cell, bundle movement pulls on tip links and opens transduction channels. Insect odorant receptors are ligand gated channels. In a free nerve ending, T R P V one senses heat in the same protein that forms the pore.
scenes.narration: In a hair cell, bundle movement pulls on tip links and opens transduction channels. Insect odorant receptors are ligand-gated channels. In a free nerve ending, TRPV1 senses heat in the same protein that forms the pore.
scenes.caption: In a hair cell, bundle movement pulls on tip links and opens transduction channels. Insect odorant receptors are ligand-gated channels. In a free nerve ending, TRPV1 senses heat in the same protein that forms the pore.
scenes.visual: Three panels: deflect a hair bundle and tension its tip links; bind an odorant to an insect odorant-receptor/Orco complex; heat a TRPV1 channel in a free nerve ending. Show a current through each open pore. Avoid assigning a receptor stoichiometry.

scenes.tts: A G protein coupled receptor puts enzymes between receptor and pore. In a rod, light activates rhodopsin, transducin and P D E six. Falling cyclic G M P closes channels and hyperpolarizes the cell. In a vertebrate olfactory neuron, rising cyclic A M P opens channels and depolarizes the cell. Cascades can amplify, but gain varies. Amplification takes time, and amplifiers also amplify noise.
scenes.narration: A G protein-coupled receptor puts enzymes between receptor and pore. In a rod, light activates rhodopsin, transducin and PDE6. Falling cGMP closes channels and hyperpolarizes the cell. In a vertebrate olfactory neuron, rising cAMP opens channels and depolarizes the cell. Cascades can amplify, but gain varies. Amplification takes time, and amplifiers also amplify noise.

Falling cGMP closes channels and hyperpolarizes the cell. In a vertebrate olfactory neuron, rising cAMP opens channels and depolarizes the cell. Cascades can amplify, but gain varies. Amplification takes time, and amplifiers also amplify noise.
scenes.visual: Compare rod and vertebrate olfactory cascades. Rod: light → rhodopsin → transducin → PDE6 → cGMP falls → CNG channels close → hyperpolarization. Olfactory: receptor → Golf → adenylyl cyclase III → cAMP rises → CNG channels open → depolarization. Mark amplification, time and noise qualitatively, with no numerical gain or speed ratio.

scenes.tts: How do we identify the channel? Speed alone is not proof. Look for the right location, loss of the native current, mutations that change permeation, and sensitivity in a new system. Kinetics must fit too. In mouse hair cells, restoring altered T M C one and chemically modifying it changed permeation rapidly, strengthening the pore argument.

scenes.visual: Replace the speed-only rule with five converging evidence cards: location, loss of native current, altered permeation, sufficiency and compatible kinetics. Illustrate the TMC1 result in mouse hair cells lacking Tmc1 and Tmc2: restore cysteine-substituted TMC1, then apply a modifying reagent and show a rapid irreversible permeation change. Do not depict this native-cell experiment as heterologous sufficiency.

scenes.tts: Now separate detection from output. Mouse type two taste cells detect sweet, bitter or umami through G protein coupled receptors. They release A T P through C A L H M one and three instead of vesicles. Deleting C A L H M three abolished taste evoked A T P release while leaving the cells excitable. The cell could respond, but could not send the message.
scenes.narration: Now separate detection from output. Mouse type II taste cells detect sweet, bitter or umami through G protein-coupled receptors. They release ATP through CALHM1/3 instead of vesicles. Deleting Calhm3 abolished taste-evoked ATP release while leaving the cells excitable. The cell could respond, but could not send the message.
scenes.caption: Now separate detection from output. Mouse type II taste cells detect sweet, bitter or umami through G protein-coupled receptors. They release ATP through CALHM1/3 instead of vesicles. scenes.visual: Show a mouse type II taste cell: sweet/bitter/umami → GPCR pathway → excitation → CALHM1/3-mediated ATP release → gustatory afferent. In a Calhm3-deletion comparison, preserve excitability but remove taste-evoked ATP output. Show channel-mediated release without vesicles; remove the activation-fraction curves and pulse calculation.

scenes.tts: Finally, ask which cell carries the signal. An olfactory neuron sends its own axon to the bulb. Hair cells and type two taste cells pass the message to a separate afferent. This is cell architecture. It is a different question from how the stimulus changes the current.

scenes.visual: Compare a primary sensory neuron, an olfactory neuron with its own axon to the bulb, with secondary receptor cells, a hair cell and type II taste cell signaling to separate afferents. End with two distinct questions: How does the stimulus change current? Which cell carries the signal?
